The Work, Teachings, and Philosophy of Scripture and Mysticism of Rabbi Elijah Benamozegh

This text surveys the multifaceted figure of Rabbi Elijah Benamozegh, an Italian thinker of the 19th century who integrated the tradition of Israel with Western philosophy and modern scholarship. The article presents his revolutionary conception granting primacy to the Oral Torah as a living foundation that establishes the Written [Torah], alongside a vigorous defense of Kabbalah and the promotion of a universal vision of Noahide religion for all humanity. The author describes the Rabbi's public activity as a printer of books in Livorno and the stormy religious polemic aroused by his bold compositions, which were burned in certain places due to their combination of biblical criticism with faith. Ultimately, the source seeks to emphasize the relevance of his original teaching as a cultural bridge offering a unique response to the crises of modernity and secularization.

The Work, Teachings, and Philosophy of Scripture and Mysticism of Rabbi Elijah Benamozegh

Introduction: His Life, Family Lineage, and the Formation of His Personality

Rabbi Elijah Benamozegh (the Raba"a), who was active in the 19th century in Livorno, Italy, represents a unique philosophical and theological voice in the landscape of Jewish and halakhic thought.[1, 2] The Raba"a was born in Livorno on April 24, 1823 (13 Iyyar 5583) and died in the same city on February 6, 1900 (7 Adar I 5660).[2] His family origins present a fusion between the profound traditions of Maghrebi Jewry and the cultural openness of Italian Jewry; his father, Abraham ben Shem Tov, was a native of Fez, Morocco, who remained childless until age 70, and married Clara at that age with the consent of his first wife.[2] The Raba"a was born to his father when he was 71.[2] His mother, Clara, was the daughter of the kabbalist dayyan Rabbi Abraham Raphael Coriat, who was born in Tétouan and was active in Mogador and Livorno.[2]

Elijah was orphaned from his mother at age four and from his father at age five, and was raised by his uncle, the great dayyan and kabbalist Rabbi Judah Coriat, who served him as a spiritual father and distinguished teacher.[2] In his youth, the Raba"a was required to engage in commerce, and worked in a local cotton warehouse.[1, 2] This period was described by him as a kind of spiritual house arrest: he was accustomed to hiding behind piles of cotton in order to read secretly the writings of Baruch Spinoza, or to conceal the books of the Italian Catholic thinker Vincenzo Gioberti under the work counter.[2] Many years later he wrote that he felt imprisoned at that time, and that time after time he set aside the account ledgers in order to grasp the books of Torah and science.[2]

Finally he abandoned the world of commerce and devoted himself entirely to Torah and philosophical research.[1] At only 18 years of age he was ordained to the rabbinate, and served as head of the beit din and as rabbi of the Livorno community for approximately fifty years.[1, 2] His general education exceeded significantly what was customary in his generation; he mastered approximately twenty languages, including Hebrew, French, Italian, Latin, Arabic, Persian, and English.[2] His mastery of the oral Torah sources was combined with expertise in Western philosophy, from the pre-Socratic philosophers to Eduard von Hartmann.[2] Most of his manuscripts, encompassing approximately 40,000 pages, were researched by Rabbi Dr. Elijah Rachamim Zayni, who was required to review approximately 10,000 books in order to decipher and explicate them.[2]

The Printing Press Enterprise in Livorno and Its Influence on the World of Torah Books

Parallel to his spiritual leadership, the Raba"a established in Livorno an independent printing house that served as a center for the dissemination of sacred books by sages of East and West.[1, 2] This enterprise enabled him to publish his own books, and also to create cultural bridges between the communities of Israel in the Mediterranean basin.[1, 2, 3] The printing house printed, among other things, the books of the sages of Morocco, Aram Tzova, Syria, and Baghdad, and thereby contributed to the preservation of the Torah creativity of the Islamic lands.[2]

Besides the production of halakhic books, the printing house served as a platform for printing communal compositions, sermons, and eulogies, such as the eulogy that the Raba"a wrote in 1873 on the occasion of the death of Cesare Castelli (Parole pronunciate nel cimitero israelitico sulla salma di Cesare Castelli) and also his Italian composition concerning the emissaries of the Holy Land (Le missioni di Terra Santa).[2, 4]

The Revolution of the Oral Torah and the Reversal of Hermeneutic Dependence

In his compositions dedicated to defending the Oral Torah, foremost among them "Mavo la-Torah she-be'al peh" [Introduction to the Oral Torah] (based on a series of articles he published in the newspaper "Ha-Levanon") and "Masoret – ve-hi Torah she-be'al peh" [Tradition – That Is the Oral Torah] (published originally in French under the title De la Tradition), the Raba"a effected a profound ontological and conceptual revolution.[2, 5] In the prevailing scholastic conception, the Written Torah is perceived as the primary text, while the Oral Torah is defined as a secondary interpretation derived from it.

The Raba"a reversed the direction of hermeneutic dependence.[2] According to his approach, the Oral Tradition is itself the primary, living, and creative source, while the Written Torah is merely a partial and reduced representation of it.[2] This revolution can be described by means of the relationship between the Written Torah (TW) and the Oral Torah (TO). Instead of the customary formula positing that the Oral Torah is derived from the Written:

TW → TO

The Raba"a posited an inverted equation, according to which the Written Torah draws its validity and very existence from within the broad space of the Oral Torah:

TO → TW or TW ⊂ TO

The Oral Torah does not constitute an external interpretation or later addition to the biblical text, but rather is the foundational basis without which the Written Torah has no practical or theological meaning.[2] The Raba"a was deeply influenced by the European Romantic conceptions of that era, which granted primacy to the unwritten folk tradition over dry written documents.[2] This approach served him as a sophisticated apologetic tool against biblical scholars and Reformers, who attempted to undermine the authority of the Sages by means of purely biblical philology.[2]

The Metaphysics of the Infinite and the Apologetic Defense of Kabbalah

Rabbi Benamozegh is considered the preeminent defender of esoteric Torah in the modern era.[1, 2] His defense found expression against two principal foci of criticism: the rationalist critique of Samuel David Luzzatto (Shadal), to which he responded in his book "Ta'am la-Shad" (employing a wordplay on the letters Shadal: "the Almighty makes Shadal foolish"), and the early critique of Rabbi Judah Aryeh of Modena in the book "Ari Nohem" [Roaring Lion], to which he responded in his composition "Eimat Mafgi'a al Ari" [Terror Falls upon the Lion].[2, 3, 6, 7]

The uniqueness of the Raba"a's defense lies in his epistemological approach: he argued that understanding Kabbalah, like higher mathematics or artistic creation, requires a special inner talent and a deep spiritual affinity for the subject.[2] According to his approach, the rationalist critique of Modena stemmed from a consciousness lacking sympathy and devoid of proper spiritual sense, and not from valid objective arguments.[2] In his book "Ta'am la-Shad," the Raba"a fashioned the debate as a hermeneutic dialogue between two figures: "Chofni" (presenting the difficulties of Shadal) and "Pinchas" (responding and representing the author's opinion), while employing the same linguistic and philological tools that Shadal himself wielded in order to prove the antiquity of the Zohar.[2]

Upon this foundation, the Raba"a developed a metaphysical doctrine that bridges between the kabbalistic concept "Ein Sof" and modern philosophical thought.[2] He argued that human intellectual impotence is the clearest proof of the existence of the Infinite, since human consciousness always senses the boundary, the mystery, and the shadows that testify to the existence of an infinite space beyond them.[2] In his composition "Spinoza and the Kabbalah," he sought to prove that Western philosophy and German idealism owe a deep debt to Jewish Kabbalah through the mediation of Spinoza.[2] According to his approach, while Kabbalah situated its metaphysical paradigms in symbolic and poetic language, Spinoza attempted to demonstrate them in a rational and dry manner.[2]

Cosmic Universalism: Israel, Christianity, and Islam

At the center of the Raba"a's later doctrine stands the aspiration for the unity of humankind, formulated in his monu-
and his work *Israël et Humanité* (Israel and Humanity) in the original French. HaRav Ben Amozegh carefully distinguished between Jewish national uniqueness (particularism) and global moral commitment (universalism). According to his system, while the people of Israel are obligated in the 613 commandments by virtue of the Sinai covenant, the other nations of the world are obligated in the seven Noahide commandments. He did not aspire to mass conversion, but rather to the correction of mythological beliefs and their integration within the universal Noahide religion, thereby restoring the divine sparks that were scattered among the seventy nations following the crisis of the Tower of Babel.

His book "Jewish Morality versus Christian Morality" (published in 1867) is structured in 12 chapters, maintaining the following thematic ratio:

Chapters of the composition = 10 Christianity + 2 Islam = 12

In these chapters, HaRav Ben Amozegh presents a comparative and ambivalent analysis of these two religions:

Christianity: HaRav Ben Amozegh attributes to it a historical contribution in spreading monotheism, but sharply criticizes its morality. According to his view, Christianity adhered to the metaphysical and religious aspect of Judaism while abolishing practical law through Paul, which led to moral anarchy and contempt for the body and the material world. Since reality necessitates political governance, a dangerous mixture arose in Christianity between church and state (religion and politics), which gave birth to oppressive phenomena such as the Inquisition.

Islam: In contrast to Christianity, Islam adopted from Judaism primarily the social and political aspects. Nevertheless, HaRav Ben Amozegh criticizes Islam for having transferred bodily desires and the pleasures of this world to the world to come, and for transforming the concept of reward and resurrection of the dead into a material continuation of physical life. He summarized this by asserting that Islam favored the political-social aspect of Judaism, while Christianity favored its religious-metaphysical aspect.

His book *Israël et Humanité* was originally published by his non-Jewish assistant, Aimé Pallière, who edited and completed the book but omitted entire passages from the original manuscript. Rabbi Dr. Zeini retranslated the book based on the complete manuscripts in order to present HaRav Ben Amozegh's doctrine without these omissions.

The *Em LaMikra* Polemic and the Rabbinic Campaign Surrounding It

The central exegetical composition of Rabbi Ben Amozegh, *Em LaMikra* (Mother of Scripture), printed in five volumes in 1862–1863, provoked a wide-ranging religious and rabbinic polemic. The book sought to defend tradition against biblical criticism by employing findings of modern research, but included three bold claims that were perceived as problematic by conservative circles:

The Theory of Ancient Scrolls: HaRav Ben Amozegh agreed with the view that before Moses there existed books or scrolls that documented the deeds of the patriarchs, and from them parts of the Torah narratives were compiled: "We permitted ourselves to agree with the opinions of those who say that before Moses there were books or scrolls... and from them the Torah narratives were compiled."

Comparison of Kabbalah to Platonic Philosophy: HaRav Ben Amozegh pointed to a distinct correspondence between ideas from the Sefer HaZohar and Plato's doctrine, and determined that the masters of esoteric knowledge and Plato were directed toward the same spiritual source.

Similarity to Ancient Egyptian Laws: He rejected Shadal's differentiating approach, and argued that there exists great similarity between Torah laws and the laws of ancient peoples, although he emphasized that the Torah refined the truth ("the food") from within idolatrous falsehood ("the waste").

These positions aroused fierce opposition among Jewish communities in the Mediterranean basin. Three years after the book's printing, in the year 5625 (1865), the rabbis of Aleppo addressed the sages of Jerusalem in a letter demanding that the volumes of the Pentateuch in which the commentary was printed be burned, after the book had already been actually burned in the Damascus community.

In response to the attacks, HaRav Ben Amozegh addressed the rabbis of Jerusalem in a letter combining ornate Hebrew with deep irony, in which he compared himself to an old man married to two women—a young one and an old one—who hate each other. The young one (representing modernity) plucks out his black hairs, and the old one (representing conservatism) plucks out his white hairs, until he is left bald on both sides. He summarized this by asserting: "I am neither assimilating nor awaiting the Messiah, neither Shammai nor Hillel, neither day nor night."

When the sages of Libya sought to excommunicate him for what was perceived in their eyes as a tendency toward biblical criticism, he responded to them reproachfully: "Why do you excommunicate only me? You must also excommunicate Ibn Ezra. What do you want from me?!" He emphasized that the investigation of historical truth does not contradict faith, and that his path rests on foundations laid by the great early authorities. In recent generations his figure has received renewed appreciation; in his weekly lesson during Hanukkah 5783, the Gaon Rabbi Meir Mazuz brought a segulah for unmarried people to marry (jumping over the Hanukkah oil bonfire on the eighth day), which he attributed to HaRav Ben Amozegh, while praising his commentaries and defining him as a philosopher and great sage worthy of reliance.

Summary and the Significance of His Doctrine for the Generations

The legacy of Rabbi Eliyahu Ben Amozegh establishes a model for the encounter between absolute halakhic and metaphysical tradition and free and critical use of modern research tools. His cross-cultural writing, created out of deep existential and intellectual duality, was ahead of its time and offered original solutions to the crises of modernity and secularization. Through the reversal of the dependency relationship between the Written Torah and the Oral Torah, the construction of a universal Noahide theology, and a philosophical defense of esoteric doctrine, HaRav Ben Amozegh sought to ensure Judaism's spiritual supremacy in the global arena.

Although he was pushed to the margins of collective memory following the fierce polemics that accompanied his life, the recent generation's research of his writings and their publication in annotated scholarly editions brings his work to the forefront of the intellectual stage of Jewish thought, and presents him as one of the most original and courageous theologians who emerged in Italian Jewry and in the Sephardic Torah world in the modern era.
